abstract.p: Effective targeted therapies for small cell lung cancer (SCLC) remain a significant challenge. Targeting the epigenome to overcome immune evasion and chemoresistance represents a promising strategy to improve treatment outcomes. In this study, we explored the role of Polycomb repressive complex 2 (PRC2), a key transcriptional repressor, by dissecting its structural and enzymatic functions. Conditional deletion of Eed, a core structural component of PRC2, prevented tumor formation in an autochthonous SCLC model. In contrast, enzymatic inhibition of EZH2 had no impact on tumor growth but significantly altered the PRC2 interactome, unveiling novel targets for drug development. Since EZH2 inhibitors are already clinically approved for other cancers, we conducted a focused combination drug screen to enhance their therapeutic potential in SCLC. Our findings revealed that prolonged EZH2 inhibition sensitized neuroendocrine cancer cells to G9a/GLP inhibition. Transcriptomic analysis revealed that the drug combination triggered an oxidative stress response by modulating the expression of cellular oxidases, an effect that could be reversed by antioxidant treatment. These results underscore the critical role of PRC2’s structural functions in SCLC and identify promising drug combinations to enhance the efficacy of EZH2 inhibitors.

Small cell lung cancer cells are dependent on the structural, but not enzymatic, function of PRC2. Combined enzymatic inhibition of PRC2 and G9a/GLP induces oxidative stress, leading to selective death of neuroendocrine SCLC cells.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Small cell lung cancer (SCLC), a highly aggressive neuroendocrine tumor, is often diagnosed at an advanced stage with metastasis, leading to a dismal 5-year survival rate of less than 7%1. The current standard-of-care treatment, including chemotherapy with Immune checkpoint blockade (ICB), offers only modest improvement in overall survival2. SCLC is characterized by substantial tumor heterogeneity, with most primary tumors retaining neuroendocrine (NE) differentiation and exhibiting immunosuppressive features such as repressed antigen presentation3,4. However, only around 15% of the patients have an inflamed tumor with functional antigen presentation and T cell infiltration, which are crucial for the success of ICB5. These tumors often develop non-neuroendocrine (non-NE) phenotype, a feature commonly associated with chemoresistance in SCLC6,7. These observations highlight the need for strategies that target the plasticity and immunogenicity of SCLC cells to improve therapeutic responses.

Recent studies have identified epigenetic alterations as central to the plasticity and chemoresistance of SCLC8,9. One key player in this context is the Polycomb repressive complex 2 (PRC2), which mediates the trimethylation of histone H3 at lysine 27 (H3K27me3), leading to transcriptional repression5,10. Genetic screens aimed at identifying regulators of major histocompatibility complex (MHC) class1 expression has highlighted PRC2 core components (EED, SUZ12 and EZH2) and other ancillary proteins including MTF2, AEBP2, and BAHD1, as critical modulators of antigen presentation11,12. Notably, enzymatic inhibition of EZH2 was sufficient to restore antigen presentation and chemosensitivity in SCLC, making it a promising target. As combination of EZH2 inhibitor with chemotherapy or other targeted therapies are being evaluated in clinical trials, understanding the precise role of PRC2 components in the pathogenesis of SCLC is essential for optimizing these strategies13.

Targeting additional epigenetic modifiers such as DOT1L or histone deacetylases can improve the therapeutic potential of EZH2 inhibition in Diffuse large B-Cell lymphoma (DLBCL)14,15. These combinations are particularly effective in derepressing the bivalent PRC2 target genes associated with cell differentiation and identity. G9a (EHMT2) is a H3K9 methyltransferase that has been shown to interact with PRC2 either through direct interaction with EZH2 or in a SUZ12 dependent manner resulting in dual repression of developmental and tumor suppressor genes16,17. Concomitant inhibition of G9a and EZH2 has been identified as a viable strategy to overcome chemoresistance in lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD)17. Interestingly, genes involved in oxidative phosphorylation and cholesterol metabolism are suppressed by G9a in multiple cell types including T cells18–20. Our earlier work has identified drugs targeting the cholesterol biosynthesis pathway as synergistic partners of EZH2 inhibitors in BAP1 deficient cancers including mesothelioma21. These findings suggest that targeting the epigenome, in combination with EZH2 inhibition, may represent a novel therapeutic approach for SCLC.

Recent investigation of mechanisms of cell death in SCLC has identified the differentiation status as a major determinant of oxidative stress response22. While NE cells are addicted to thioredoxin pathway, the non-NE adherent cells have an altered lipidome rendering them sensitive to lipid peroxidation associated ferroptosis. Prolonged inhibition of EZH2 in suspension growing NE-SCLC cells is sufficient to promote adherent growth and loss of NE differentiation5. Such a change in phenotype could introduce targetable cell-intrinsic vulnerabilities. In this study, we first dissect the importance of the structural and enzymatic functions of PRC2 in SCLC using relevant preclinical models. We then explore the potential of developing drug combinations by leveraging the temporal effect of EZH2 inhibition in SCLC differentiation.

sec.title: PRC2 is essential for SCLC tumorigenesis
sec.p: Inactivation of tumor suppressors Rb1 and Trp53 in the lungs is sufficient to initiate SCLC in mice23. To investigate the role of PRC2 towards SCLC formation, we generated Rb1flox;Trp53flox;Eedflox (RPE) mice where Cre-recombinase can delete exons 3–6 of Eed (a core component of PRC2) in addition to deletion of Rb1 and Trp53 (Figure. S1A)24,25. This enables ablation of PRC2 function from tumor initiation.

Histological analysis of the lungs of PRC2-proficient Rb1flox;Trp53flox(RP) mice 20 weeks post tumor-initiation revealed SCLC lesions in the bronchiolar compartment of the lungs (Fig. 1A, B). These RP lesions retained the expression of neuroendocrine (NE) markers (Synaptophysin & CGRP) and lacked the squamous differentiation marker Cytokeratin10 (Fig. 1B & Fig. S1B, C). RP lesions displayed tri-methylation of histone H3k27 (H3k27me3), indicating active PRC2 function. In contrast, no SCLC lesions were observed in the lungs of PRC2-impaired RPE mice. Instead, clusters of cells were observed in the alveolar compartment of the lungs. They showed rich cytoplasm with blurred cell membrane and large nuclei with clear nuclear membrane. These clusters were negative for NE markers and partially positive for Cytokeratin10, suggesting non-NE lesions. Levels of H3k27me3 was diminished in RPE clusters, confirming a loss of PRC2 function. Additionally, the RPE lesions exhibited lower Ki67 levels, indicating reduced proliferative capacity compared to RP tumors (Fig. S1C, D).Fig. 1EED is essential for tumorigenesis.

LUAD cell lines are shown in red. Neuroendocrine (NE) SCLC cells are shown in green. Non-NE SCLC cell lines are shown in blue. All data is shown as mean ± SD.

To assess whether these clusters could develop into tumors, we followed the mice until their survival endpoint. While all RP mice succumbed to SCLC, only one RPE mouse developed SCLC, and two RPE mice developed non-SCLC cancers (Fig. 1A). Of the two non-SCLC cancers, one was found in the alveolar compartment of the lung resembling features of lung adenocarcinoma and the other was found outside the lungs. The remaining ten RPE mice did not develop tumors, resulting in significantly increased survival compared to RP mice (Fig. 1C). These findings suggest that the RPE clusters were benign, and that deletion of Eed impairs SCLC formation.

Cell line derived from the single SCLC RPE tumor (C584) grew as suspension cells in culture, consistent with NE differentiation. This tumor retained the expression of NE marker Synaptophysin and stained positive for H3k27me3 indicating active PRC2 function (Fig. S1E). Genomic analysis revealed both an intact and an excised Eed allele, indicating incomplete deletion of Eed in this tumor (Fig. S1F). Transfection of C584 cells with adenovirus carrying Cre-recombinase resulted in complete deletion of remaining Eed allele (Fig. S1G). This led to a significant reduction in cell survival, accompanied by increased staining for cell death markers Annexin V and PI (Fig. 1D, E). This suggests that Eed deletion is deleterious to SCLC cell survival. To further explore the role of EED in SCLC, we treated a panel of mouse (RPKO1&2) and human (H69, H82, H187, DMS114, SW1271, and DMS273) SCLC cell lines with an EED-PROTAC degrader. Treatment with the EED-PROTAC significantly reduced SCLC cell survival but did not affect the survival of lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) cells (KP141, A549, and PC9) (Fig. 1F, G). These results confirm that EED is crucial for the formation and survival of SCLC.

sec.title: PRC2 enzymatic inhibition is dispensable for SCLC
sec.p: EZH2 inhibitors (EZH2i) are approved for patients with subtypes of B-cell lymphoma and sarcoma26. To investigate if enzymatic inhibition of PRC2 using EZH2i can recapitulate EED depletion in SCLC, we treated SCLC cell lines with two different EZH2 inhibitors (GSK126 or Tazemetostat). At a concentration of 5 μM, both inhibitors successfully reduced H3k27me3 without degrading EZH2 or EED (Fig. S2A). Unlike EED depletion, short-term EZH2 inhibition for 4 days had a modest effect on survival of SCLC (Fig. S2B, C). All the cell lines tested were either completely resistant to Tazemetostat or were sensitive to GSK126 at concentrations greater than 5 μM. This data is consistent with the findings from Genomics of Drug Sensitivity in Cancer (GDSC) database27, where B-cell lymphoma cell lines (IC50mean = 6.52 μM) were more vulnerable to EZH2i (GSK343) compared to SCLC cell lines (IC50mean = 18.18 μM) (Fig. S2D). This shows that short-term 4-day EZH2 inhibition is tolerated in SCLC cell lines.

Given that prolonged EZH2 inhibition has been shown to increase antigen presentation and decrease NE differentiation in SCLC5, we examined transcriptomic changes upon extended inhibition of EZH2. Prolonged inhibition of EZH2 for 11 days resulted in greater transcriptional changes compared to short-term EZH2 inhibition (Fig. 2A). Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) revealed activation of pathways associated with keratinization and antigen processing and presentation (APP) (Fig. 2B). To assess the impact of prolonged EZH2 inhibition on proliferation, we treated SCLC cells with EZH2i over 14 days. Prolonged exposure to a lower dose of 5uM GSK126 or Tazemetostat reduced their proliferation (Fig. 2C, D). We then tested the potential of EZH2i in H69 (neuroendocrine) and DMS 273 (non-neuroendocrine) xenograft models of SCLC. Treatment of tumor bearing mice with Tazemetostat reduced H3k27me3 without depleting EZH2 in both the preclinical models tested (Fig. S2E–H). However, there was no improvement in the overall survival of mice (Fig. 2E, F). Thus, we conclude that targeting PRC2 enzymatic activity as a monotherapy is ineffective in SCLC.Fig. 2Compound-based screen to identify effective combinations with EZH2 inhibition.

sec.title: Prolonged EZH2 inhibition introduces targetable epigenetic vulnerabilities in SCLC
sec.p: As combinations with EZH2 inhibitors are being tested for various cancers, we conducted a focused drug combination screen in SCLC to identify therapeutically relevant drug targets. We used a selective panel of twelve drugs, including known effective targets in SCLC or synergistic partners of EZH2i in other cancers (Supplementary Data 1). The screen was designed in two formats: a pretreatment format where cells were treated with 5uM EZH2i (GSK126 or Tazemetostat) for 8 days, followed by combinations with varying doses of the second drug for 4 days; and a shorter non-pretreated format where cells were treated with both drugs for 4 days. If the IC50 of the second drug in combination with EZH2i was less than half of the IC50 as single agent, it was considered for further investigation.

Navitoclax, a BCL-2 inhibitor, was effective in EZH2i pretreated H69 but not in H82 (Fig. 2G, H & Supplementary Data 2), consistent with the higher expression of BCL2 in H69 (Fig. S2I)28. Similarly, JQ1 (BET bromodomain inhibitor) was more effective in pretreated H82 cells, in line with the higher expression of the drug targets BRD2&4 (Fig. S2J). Pretreated H69 and H82 cells were both more sensitive to one HDAC inhibitor (Panobinostat) but not another HDAC inhibitor (Vorinostat) (Fig. S3A–D).

Pretreatment with EZH2i sensitized both H69 and H82 cells to UNC0642 (G9a/GLP inhibitor) (Fig. 2G, H). G9a (EHMT2) and GLP (EHMT1) are histone methyl transferases that catalyze H3k9 methylation resulting in transcriptional repression. Expression of both G9a and GLP are highly elevated in SCLC cell lines making them plausible drug targets. Analysis of the results of the screen without pretreatment revealed that Prima-1 met, a mutant p53 activator, was effective in combination with EZH2i in H69 cells. However, high doses ( > 40 μM) of prima-1 met was necessary to achieve this effect making it unsuitable for further testing in preclinical models of SCLC. Our observations from the drug screen suggest that sustained EZH2 inhibition sensitizes SCLC selectively to G9a/GLP inhibition.

sec.title: NE-SCLC is sensitive to combined EZH2 and G9a/GLP inhibition
sec.p:
To validate our screening results, we tested two different G9a/GLP inhibitors (UNC0642 and UNC0638) in combination with EZH2i in SCLC cell lines. Pretreatment with EZH2i sensitized the neuroendocrine SCLC cell lines (H69, H82, and H187) to both the G9a/GLP inhibitors (Fig. 3A, B). However, no such effect was observed in non-neuroendocrine (non-NE) SCLC cell lines (DMS273, DMS114, and SW1271) (Fig. S3E–H). DMS114 and SW1271 were recently identified as SMARCA4-deficient YAP1-expressing non-NE SCLC cells29. Analysis of G9a and GLP expression revealed no correlation with NE markers (ASCL1, Synaptophysin, and NEUROD1), suggesting that differential sensitivity was not related to their expression levels (Fig. S3I).Fig. 3Prolonged EZH2 inhibition sensitizes NE-SCLC cells to G9a/GLP inhibition.
A, B Dose response curve of (with and without pretreatment) NE (H69, H82 & H187) and non-NE (DMS 273) SCLC cells to G9a/GLP inhibitors UNC0642 or UNC0638. (n = 3). C Kaplan-Meier graph showing the percentage survival of H69 xenograft model treated with vehicle (n = 8), GSK126 (n = 7), UNC0642(n = 7) or combination(n = 7). X-axis depicts the days post treatment initiation. Median survival in days for each treatment arm is mentioned in the table. D Enrichment graph for proteins more proximal to EZH2 in EZH2 inhibitor (GSK126 or Tazemetostat) treated cells compared to DMSO. This was performed using proximity labeling assay and analyzed for proteins with a minimum tenfold enrichment and p value < 0.05 in EZH2 versus IgG antibody conditions. (n = 3). E Enrichment of indicated proteins in EZH2 pulldown compared to IgG for DMSO, GSK126 and Tazemetostat treated conditions. All data is shown as mean ± SD.

Transcriptomic analysis of cells treated with G9a/GLP inhibitor revealed significant changes in 337 genes, most of which were upregulated. GSEA indicated that enriched gene sets were primarily associated with metabolic pathways, including lipid and hormone metabolism (Fig. S3J). This is consistent with previous reports showing elevated lipid metabolism and intracellular cholesterol in T cells upon G9a/GLP inhibition18. Previous work from our lab identified that targeting the cholesterol biosynthesis pathway was synergistic with EZH2i in mesothelioma21. Hence, we tested if the combination of G9a/GLP and EZH2 inhibitors is effective in mesothelioma. In mesothelioma cells, EZH2 inhibition had a minimal effect on the sensitivity to G9a/GLP inhibition (Fig. S3K). These findings confirm that NE-SCLC cells are uniquely vulnerable to the combination of EZH2 and G9a/GLP inhibition.

We then tested the combination of UNC0642 with GSK126 or Tazemetostat in xenograft models of SCLC. While the combination of GSK126 + UNC0642 was well tolerated, Tazemetostat+UNC0642 was not (Fig. S3L). We then tested the tolerated drug combination on H69 xenograft model of SCLC. Consistent with our previous results, GSK126 as a single agent was ineffective in improving the survival of the mice (Fig. 3C). UNC0642 as a single agent had a modest effect on the survival of the mice. However, treating the tumor bearing mice simultaneously with both drugs was more effective in improving the median survival from 22 days in vehicle group to 32 days in the treatment group. Further identification of biomarkers associated with pretreatment of EZH2i that improves the sensitivity to G9a/GLP, can identify the optimal sequential dosing schedule for the combination in preclinical models of SCLC.

sec.title: Combination treatment induces an oxidative stress response in NE-SCLC
sec.p: Interaction between G9a and PRC2 complex members has been previously reported to mediate drug resistance in NSCLC and promote prostate cancer progression16,17. Hence, we investigated if PRC2 enzymatic inhibition in SCLC cells could alter its interactome. For this, we performed a proximity labeling assay in SCLC cells using the ProtA-Turbo enzyme targeting EZH2 with an antibody and identified EZH2-proximal proteins using quantitative mass spectrometry30. As expected, we identified all the canonical members of PRC2 complex as significant interactors using the EZH2 antibody (Fig. S4A & Supplementary Data 3). Analysis of the proteins that had a significant interaction with EZH2 compared to IgG in EZH2i treated cells but not in DMSO treated cells, revealed an enrichment of nuclear proteins that included histone acetylases (Fig. 3D & Fig. S4B). The interaction of G9a (EHMT2) and GLP (EHMT1) with EZH2 was observed in SCLC cells (Fig. 3E). However, treatment with EZH2 inhibitors did not alter the binding of EZH2 with EED, G9a and GLP. Instead, MOZ/MORF complex that promotes acetylation of histone H3 was highly enriched in EZH2 proximity proteome in EZH2i treated cells (Fig. 3D). Interestingly, KAT6A (MOZ) catalyzed H3k9 acetylation in AML cells resulting in leukemogenic gene-expression31. Of note, the interaction of DOT1L with EZH2 was strengthened upon EZH2 inhibition. DOT1L and KAT6A have been proposed as interesting therapeutic targets in other cancers15. Our results suggest that investigating novel interactors of EZH2 upon enzymatic inhibition can identify potential synthetic lethal partners of EZH2.

Transcriptomic analysis of cells treated with combination revealed a significant difference between pretreated combination and non-pretreated combination (Fig. 4A). GSEA revealed activation of apoptosis related pathway in pretreated combination, consistent with the observed effect on cell survival (Fig. S4C). Also, gene sets associated with NFE2L2 activation, a central regulator of antioxidant response, were strongly enriched in cells treated with short term combination (Fig. S4D)32. The expression of multiple cellular oxidases were dysregulated in combination treated cells. ALOX15B is a lipid oxidase whose expression is strongly elevated following G9a/GLP inhibition or combination treatment (Fig. 4B & Fig. S4E)33. NOX4 is an ER and mitochondria associated NADPH oxidase whose expression is strongly elevated by sustained EZH2 inhibition. This is consistent with previous reports that identified NOX4 expression to be regulated by H3k27me334. Markers of oxidative stress such as HMOX1, MAFF, CHAC1 and SLC7A11 were enhanced in pretreated combination cells indicating the presence of underlying oxidative stress. Hence, we hypothesized that sustained EZH2 inhibition sensitized the cells to oxidative stress enhanced by G9a/GLP inhibition.Fig. 4Combination treatment of EZH2i and G9a/GLP inhibitor induces oxidative stress in NE-SCLC cells.

B q-PCR data of oxidative stress associated genes on DMSO or 5uM GSK126 pretreated H69 cells treated with the indicated drugs. HPRT mRNA level was used to normalize the data. (n = 3). C FACS analysis of oxidative stress in pretreated NE and non-NE SCLC cells. Cell Rox green was used to probe the ROS levels. Data was normalized to mode. D, E Cell viability assay performed on DMSO and EZH2i pretreated NE-SCLC cells. Cells were treated with 10 mM NAC (anti-oxidant). Percentage survival was normalized to DMSO control conditions. (n = 3) All data is shown as mean ± SD.

Cellular oxidative stress, measured by CellRox green dye, was elevated in pretreated combination for NE-SCLC cells (H69 and H82). This was not observed with prolonged EZH2 inhibition or G9a/GLP inhibition as a single agent (Fig. 4C). On the contrary, the combination was not effective in inducing oxidative stress in non-NE SCLC cells (DMS 273). This is consistent with the lethal effect of the combination in NE cells but not non-NE cells. Treating the cells with antioxidant, N-acetyl-L-Cysteine (NAC), rescued the effect of the combination on NE-SCLC cell survival (Fig. 4D, E & Fig. S4F). This suggests that the oxidative stress induced by the combination is responsible for the observed effect on cell death. Collectively, our results show that treating NE-SCLC cells with EZH2 inhibition sensitizes the cells to G9a/GLP inhibition by inducing oxidative stress.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: Identification of PRC2 as an essential regulator of antigen presentation and chemosensitivity in SCLC has sparked renewed interest in targeting the epigenome of SCLC. Despite the promise, clinical trials testing the combinations of EZH2 enzymatic inhibitors with chemotherapy have had limited success13. One possible explanation is the discovery of non-canonical functions of PRC2 components that might influence tumor progression in ways not targeted by conventional enzymatic inhibitors35. Our study delineates the difference between the importance of PRC2 structural activity and enzymatic activity towards the formation and maintenance of SCLC. We show that deletion of Eed impairs the formation of SCLC. A similar effect was also seen in genetic models of medulloblastoma36. Pharmacological depletion of EZH2 but not its enzymatic inhibition has been shown to promote the degradation of MYC(N) resulting in impaired growth of neuroblastoma and SCLC tumors37. Collectively, these results provide a rationale to test degraders of PRC2 complex such as PROTACs for patients with cancers of neuronal differentiation.

We show that pretreatment of NE SCLC cells with EZH2i, synergizes the cells to G9a/GLP inhibition. To reflect this synergy in preclinical models, sequential treatment of GSK126 and UNC0642 would uncover the true translational potential of our combination. However, the feasibility of such an approach is limited by the lack of an appropriate biomarker to indicate the ideal time point to begin UNC0642 treatment. Also, given the highly aggressive nature of our model, pretreatment with GSK126 for 8 days would not provide sufficient time to study the effect of UNC0642. One possible solution for this challenge is to first pretreat the cell in vitro and then transplant the cells in vivo. However, this does not represent the true clinical setting and hence was not pursued.

Our work identified that the interactome of EZH2 significantly changes following enzymatic inhibition. Multiple epigenetic regulators of transcription such as KAT6A and DOT1L were identified as novel interactors. Though this could partly contribute towards the inherent resistance to EZH2 inhibition, they also offer new opportunities to develop synergistic drug combinations. A recent study investigating resistance to EZH2 inhibition in B cell lymphoma identified DOT1L to contribute towards EZH2i sensitivity15. Combined inhibition of EZH2 and DOT1L restricted the activation of MYC pathway resulting in loss of pro-proliferative germinal center differentiation. On a similar note, direct interaction of G9a with EZH2 has been identified to mediate drug resistance in LUAD17. However, investigation of advanced prostate cancer, a cancer that develops neuroendocrine differentiation upon progression, has identified a PRC2 accessory protein PALI1 to mediate the interaction of G9a with SUZ12 resulting in dual H3k27me3 and H3k9me2 mediated repression of cell differentiation16. Hence, identifying direct and indirect interactors of EZH2 using extensive techniques such as proximity labeling assay might provide additional relevant drug targets compared to a traditional antibody-based co-immunoprecipitation approach.

Differentiation therapy is highly successful in treating certain cancers like leukemias and holds promise for drug-resistant tumors38. This approach often involves treatment with drug(s) that effects a phenotypic change resulting in either cell death or inducing a targetable vulnerability. Treating NE-SCLC cells with EZH2i results in loss of NE differentiation and restores antigen presentation, which can improve their sensitivity to immune checkpoint blockade5. We show that such a treatment with EZH2i can also induce vulnerability to G9a regulated oxidative stress. Though extrinsic apoptosis mediated by caspase-8 is suppressed in all subtypes of SCLC, non-NE SCLC cells are vulnerable to ferroptosis, a type of regulated necrosis associated with lipid peroxidation22. Analysis of lipid metabolism has identified increased presence of ether-linked polyunsaturated fatty acids in non-NE cells compared to NE cells, rendering them sensitive to ferroptosis22. We observe a strong induction of lipid oxidases such as ALOX15B following G9a inhibition which could explain the increased sensitivity after pretreatment with EZH2i. Also, dual EZH2 and G9a inhibition has been shown to induce ER-stress mediated reactive oxygen species in multiple myeloma20,39, suggesting that this might be a broader target in various cancers. Radiation therapy has been an effective tool in managing all stages of SCLC40. As radiation therapy is a potent inducer of oxidative stress response including ferroptosis41, investigation of EZH2i as neoadjuvant therapy for radiation could hold promise for improving the prognosis of SCLC patients. Indeed, targeting EZH2 reduced the radio-resistance in bladder cancer cells42.

In conclusion, our findings show that the presence of PRC2 structural component EED is critical for the formation and progression of SCLC, whereas the enzymatic activity of PRC2 is dispensable. Treating NE-SCLC cells with EZH2 inhibitors sensitizes the cells to oxidative stress enhanced by G9a/GLP inhibition.

sec.title: Cell culture
sec.p: Human SCLC cell lines NCI-H69, NCI-H187, NCI-H82 and DMS273 (kindly provided by lab of Prof. Anton Berns, NKI and were initially acquired from American Type Culture Collection (ATCC)) were cultured in Dulbecco’s Modified Eagle Medium/Nutrient Mixture F-12 (DMEM/F12+Glutamax; Gibco), supplemented with 4 μg/ml Hydrocortisone (Sigma), 5 ng/ml murine EFG (Sigma), insulin-transferrin-selenium solution (ITS; Gibco), 10% fetal calf serum (FCS; Capricorn), and 1% penicillin and streptomycin (Gibco). Murine cell lines were isolated from fresh tumors developed from autochthonous model and cultured in the same medium. Human SCLC cell lines (DMS114 and SW1271) and mesothelioma cell lines (H2731, H2810, and H2818) were obtained from ATCC and cultured in the same medium as above. RPKO1 and RPKO2 cell lines were derived in-house from 2 different RP tumors. The tumors were chopped in trypsin, and the floating cells were cultured and passaged. KP141 cells were generated in-house and mentioned in ref. 24. C584 cell lines was derived in-house from RPE tumors. The tumor was chopped in trypsin, and the floating cells were cultured and passaged. A549 was obtained from ATCC and PC9 cells were a gift from Prof. Rene Bernards group at NKI43. All cell lines were cultured in 37 °C humidified incubator with 5% carbon dioxide. These cell lines were tested negative for mycoplasma contamination using mycoalert mycoplasma detection kit (Lonza).

sec.title: Animal studies
sec.p: Animal experiments were approved by the Institutional committees (Animal experimental committee and welfare body) at the Netherlands Cancer Institute as per Dutch law. We have complied with all relevant ethical regulations for animal use. All mice were housed in specific pathogen free environment with standard feeding, light and temperature conditions.

For xenograft models, 1*10^6 cells of H69 or DMS273 were diluted in 100ul of 50% Matrigel (Corning) in sterile PBS (GIBCO). This was then implanted subcutaneously into the flank of 6–10-week-old NOD-Scid-IL2Rgnull (NSG) mice (Jackson Laboratory). Tumor volume was measured every 2–3 days by caliper measurement. Mice were weighed every other day and checked for signs of illness. Mice were randomized into control and treatment groups before the start of therapeutic intervention. For Tazemetostat (MedKoo Biosciences) treatment as monotherapy, mice bearing tumors of volume~50mm3 were treated with 300 mg/kg b.i.d orally for 28 days. For combination treatment, GSK126 (40 mg/kg, MedKoo Biosciences) and UNC0642 (10 mg/kg, MedKoo Biosciences) were dissolved in 20% Captisol and administered intraperitoneally once every day for 28 days. Mice were followed regularly until they reached the humane end point (tumor volume of 1500 mm3 or breathing problems or 15% body weight loss or kyphosis). For experiments investigating Tazemetostat as monotherapy (Fig. 2E, F), statistical analysis was performed between control (Vehicle) and Tazemetostat group. For experiments investigating combination treatment (Fig. 3C), statistical analysis was performed between control (Vehicle) and other treatment groups. The primary outcomes assessed were the effect of treatment on the survival of the mouse and the tumor volume. Each data point indicates a separate mouse. To achieve a difference of 500mm3 of tumor volume with a standard deviation of 20%, we calculate an anticipated effect size (cohen’s d) of 1.6. Sample size was calculated with a desired statistical power of 0.8 and a error rate of 5% using a A-PRIORI sample size calculator for student t-test. There was no inclusion or exclusion criteria established. Mice were excluded only if the cause of death was unrelated to tumor burden or treatment toxicity. The mice were randomly assigned to control or treatment groups, with groups balanced for sex. The order of treatment and animal locations was determined randomly by the personal at the intervention core facility (IVD) and this was not influenced by the authors designing the experiment. The maximum tumor size permitted by the ethics committee was 1500mm3. Mice were sacrificed immediately after the tumor volume reached 1500mm3. The maximum tumor size was not exceeded beyond 1500 mm3.

For autochthonous models, 8 week old Rb1flox;Trp53flox;Eedflox (RPE) and Rb1flox;Trp53flox(RP) FVB mice were intra-tracheally infected with 50ul of 10^9 pfu/ml adenovirus carrying CMV-Cre recombinase construct. Mice were monitored for signs of illness every 2–3 days and were sacrificed upon reaching the above-mentioned humane end point. Genotyping of the tissues were performed by PCR. Primers used for Rb1 and Trp53 floxed alleles are mentioned in previous study23. Primers used for Eed floxed and excised alleles are mentioned in the previous study from our lab25. Tissues and organs including lungs were collected and fixed in EAF fixative, from which paraffin blocks and sections were made according to routine procedure. For IHC, antibodies were applied as following: synaptophysin (abcam; ab32127, at 1:10000), H3K27me3 (BioLegend; 905401, at 1:500), CGRP (Sigma, C8198, at 1:500), Ki67 (abcam, ab15580, at 1:2000) and cytokeratin10 (abcam; ab6002, at 1:100). Statistical analysis is performed between control (RP) and Eed knockout group (RPE). Each data point indicates a separate mouse. The primary outcomes assessed were the effect of Eed deletion on morphology of the disease and survival of mouse. For survival comparisons between groups, an a priori power calculation was performed using GPower v3.1 (t tests: difference between two independent means, two-tailed). The assumed effect size was d = 1.3, with a significance level (α) of 0.05 and an intended power of 0.9. An allocation ratio of 1:1 was specified. The sample size was calculated to achieve power of 0.80. Both male and female mice with the correct genotype were used for this experiment. There was no inclusion or exclusion criteria established. No mouse that received cre-recombinase was excluded from the analysis. The mice selected for early-stage time points and survival analysis were determined electronically in a completely random manner and by the personal at the intervention core facility (IVD). The animals with different genotypes were housed in separate cages, but the location of the cages were completely randomized by IVD. The tumor volume for the autochthonous model was not measured as the tumors originated within the lungs. The ethics committee approved the humane end point as incidence of breathing problems or 15% body weight loss or kyphosis. Mice were sacrificed immediately if any of the humane end points were observed. The humane end point was not exceeded in this experiment.

All animal experiments were designed by the authors and performed in a blinded manner by the personal at the intervention core facility (IVD). Animal handlers allocated the mice to different groups, conducted the experiment and measured the outcome independently. The outcome was shared with the authors. The analysis of survival data, immunohistochemistry and ex vivo data was performed by the authors. All mice were transported to the corresponding caging facility atleast one week before the start of the experiment to avoid confounding issues including stress on the animal. This is a standard practice followed by the IVD. All the animal experiments were performed only after the protocols were registered and approved by the regulation committee. The protocol numbers are (A) 9.2.9379 (autochthonous model with Eed deletion) (B) 24.1.10197 (Tazemetostat as monotherapy) (C) 24.1.11264 (MTD studies) (D) 24.1.11425 (EZH2i G9a/GLPi combination studies). In all protocols, the mice were sacrificed immediately after the humane end point was reached. The source data for all the mouse experiments is provided in Supplementary Data 4.

sec.title: Drug and cell viability studies
sec.p: H69, DMS273, H187 (6000ul/well) and H82 (10,000 cells/well) cell lines were optimized for the seeding density and plated in 50 μl/well in a 384 well plate. Cells were exposed to drugs for 4 days for cell viability studies. DMSO was used for negative control and phenylarsine oxide (PAO) was used as positive control for cell death. Drugs were dispensed using D300e digital dispenser (TECAN). Cell viability was measured after 4-h incubation with Resazurin (Sigma) using M1000 pro plate reader (TECAN). Dose response curves were plotted using GraphPad Prism version 10. Data was analyzed and IC50 was calculated using Nonlinear regression curve fit on GraphPad Prism.

Focused drug screen was performed with target drug library in two different formats. For pretreatment arm, 3*10^5 cells were seeded in each well of 6-well plate with 3 ml of medium. Cells were treated with 5 μM GSK126, Tazemetostat or DMSO. Every 3 days, the cells were trypsinized and transferred into plates of higher volume with fresh drugs. After 8 days of pretreatment, H69 and H82 cells were diluted in medium containing 5uM EZH2i or DMSO and plated in 384 well plates. For short-term arm or without pretreatment, fresh H69 and H82 cells were diluted in medium containing 5 μM EZH2i or DMSO and plated in 384 well plate. Varying doses of target drug library was added to both the treatment arms using the drug dispenser. Cell viability was measure after 4days and IC50 was calculated for every drug individually either in the presence or absence of EZH2i.

sec.title: Western blot
sec.p: RIPA buffer containing 50 mM Tris-HCl, pH 7.4, 150 mM NaCl, 1.0% NP-40, 0.5% sodium deoxycholate, 0.1% SDS, 2 mM EDTA, 1 mM Sodium orthovanadate, and protease inhibitor complete cocktail (Roche) was used to lyse the cell pellets. Protein concentration was measured by Protein assay dye reagent (Biorad) using Nanodrop 2000c spectrophotometer (Thermofisher). Western blot was performed using 4-12% Bis-Tris gels (NuPage-Novex, Invitrogen) and proteins were then transferred onto nitrocellulose membranes (0.2 μM, Whatman). Membranes were blocked using 5% bovine serum albumin (Sigma) in PBS with 0.1% Tween-20. Following 30 min of blocking, membranes were exposed to primary antibodies overnight at 4 degrees in fresh blocking buffer. Antibodies used were Vinculin (V9131), beta-tubulin (sc5274), EZH2 (D2C9, Cell Signaling, 5246 T), EED (Millipore, 05-1320) and H3k27me3 (Millipore, 07-449). Membranes were then washed and treated with secondary antibodies conjugated to HRP. Gels were then exposed to Amersham ECL detection reagent prior to imaging using ChemiDoc XRS+ (BioRad).

sec.title: RNA extraction and RT q-PCR
sec.p: ReliaPrep (Promega) was used for RNA extraction from cell pellets. Reverse transcription was performed using Tetro cDNA synthesis kit (Meridian) with random hexamer primers. Power SYBR green master mix (Applied biosystems) was used to perform qPCR, and signal was measured using Quantstudio 5 real-time PCR system (Thermofisher). HPRT was used as control for each sample measured. Primers used:
HPRT (for- CGAGATGTGATGAAGGAGATGG, rev-TTGATGTAATCCAGCAGGTCAG),
NOX4 (for- CAGATGTTGGGGCTAGGATTG, rev-GAGTGTTCGGCACATGGGTA),
ALOX15B (for- CTGAATGGTCTCAACCCTGTC, rev-GGGAGCCCTTCTCTAGCTCA),
HMOX1 (for- CCAGGCAGAGAATGCTGAGTTC, rev-AAGACTGGGCTCTCCTTGTTGC),
MAFF (for- CTGTCGGACGAGGCGCTGATG, rev- AGCCACGGTTTTTGAGTGTGCG),
CHAC1 (for- GAACCCTGGTTACCTGGGC, rev- CGCAGCAAGTATTCAAGGTTGT) and SLC7A11 (for- TCTCCAAAGGAGGTTACCTGC, rev- AGACTCCCCTCAGTAAAGTGAC).

sec.title: RNA-sequencing
sec.p: H69 cells were pretreated with 5 μM GSK126 or DMSO for 8 days. Fresh H69 and pretreated H69 cells were subsequently treated for 3 days with DMSO, 5uM EZH2i, 5uM UNC0642 or combination. Cells were then lysed in RLT buffer (Qiagen). RNA extraction, library preparation, sequencing, and reads processing were performed by the Genomics Core Facility at the Netherlands Cancer Institute. Sequencing was performed using the Illumina HiSeq 2500 platform according to the standard procedures. Sequencing reads were aligned to GRCh38 and read counts per gene using gensum. Genes were annotated using Ensembl GRCh38.102. Subsequent data analyses were performed using R and Bioconductor. DESeq2 (v1.44.0) package was used for the analysis of differential gene expression44. Pre-filtering was performed by removing all genes with less or equal to 10 total reads. DESeq2 was also used to retrieve log2-transformed, normalized transcript counts, which were subsequently used for visualization purposes.

For GSEA, genes were ranked on fold change estimates after shrinkage of effect size using DESeq2. Next, GSEA was performed using the fgsea package (v1.30.0) with default settings and nPermSimple set to 100,000. Relevant gene sets were retrieved using the msigdb package (v1.12.0) (10.18129/B9.bioc.msigdb).

The raw sequence data reported in this paper have been deposited in the Genome Sequence Archive (Genomics, Proteomics & Bioinformatics 2025) in National Genomics Data Center45, China National Center for Bioinformation / Beijing Institute of Genomics, Chinese Academy of Sciences (GSA-Human: HRA013579) that are publicly accessible at https://ngdc.cncb.ac.cn/gsa-human.

sec.title: Proximity labeling assay
sec.p: ProtA-TurboID experiments were performed as mentioned in ref. 30 and also discussed here. H69 cells were cultured in 15-cm dishes and treated with 5 μM EZH2i or DMSO for 8 days. Fresh cell pellets (20*10^6 cells) were washed in wash buffer (20 mM HEPES pH 7.5, 150 mM NaCl, 0.5 mM spermidine and CPI). Cells are then resuspended in 500 μl of Digitonin buffer (0.04% digitonin in wash buffer). They were rotated for 10 min at room temperature (RT) using a rotator (ELMI Intelli-Mixer RM-2M) at 10 rpm. Cell permeabilization was then measured using trypan blue to ensure a viability of less than 20%. Cells were then suspended in 200 μl of digitonin buffer with 2 μl of IgG or EZH2 (D2C9, Cell Signaling, 5246 T) antibody. Samples were then incubated in a thermoshaker at 600 rpm at RT for 20 min. After washing, samples were then incubated with 1.4 μg of ProtA-Turbo in 300 μl of digitonin buffer for 30 min at 4 oC and 10 rpm. Cells were then resuspended in 300 μl of fresh biotinylation buffer (5 mM of MgCl2, 5 μM biotin, 1 mM ATP prepared in digitonin buffer) for 30 min at 500 rpm at 37 oC. Cells were then washed and resuspended in RIPA buffer at 4 oC overnight. Cells were then sonicated (NGS Bioruptor) for 30 s on/ 30 s off cycles until transparent. This was then centrifuged, and the supernatant was treated with streptavidin Sepharose beads for 2 h at RT. Beads were then collected and the bound proteins were trypsinized. The eluates were collected, acidified and purified on C18 stagetips followed by liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry.

sec.title: Liquid chromatography/mass spectrometry
sec.p: LC-MS/MS was performed by nanoLC-MS/MS on an Orbitrap Astral mass spectrometer (Thermo Scientific) connected to a Vanquish Neo nano-LC system (Thermo Scientific). The Vanquish Neo was operated in the trap-and-elute mode, and peptides were loaded onto a Pepmap 100 C18 5 µm trap column (300 µm x 5 mm, Thermo Scientific), before separation on the analytical column (AUR3-25075C18-TS, 1.7 µm/75 µm x 25 cm, IonOpticks AU) mounted into an Easyspray ion source (Thermo Scientific) with 1350 V spray voltage applied. The column was heated to 50 0C and the flow rate was set to 0.5 µL/min at the start of the method to minimize delay time. Solvent A was 0.1% formic acid/water and solvent B was 0.1% formic acid/80% acetonitrile. Peptides were eluted at a flow rate of 0.4 µL/min in a 36-min effective gradient, containing a non-linear increase from 8 to 45% solvent B, followed by a 0.4-min ramp to 99% solvent B and 5.4-min wash at 0.5 µL/min flow rate at the end. The column was finally equilibrated using the “fast equilibration” script in combined control mode with a 1450 bar pressure limit. The Orbitrap Astral was run in data-independent acquisition (DIA) mode, with full MS scans being collected in the Orbitrap analyzer with 240,000 resolution at m/z 200 over a 380–980 m/z range. Default charge state was 2 + , the normalized AGC target was set to 500% (equivalent to 5e6 charges) and the maximum injection time was 5 ms. For DIA MS2, a normalized HCD collision energy of 25% was applied to a 380–980 m/z precursor range using non-overlapping isolation windows of 2Th, with window placement optimization turned on. Scans were acquired in the Astral analyzer over a 100-1000 m/z range, with the normalized AGC target set to 500% (equivalent to 5e4 charges) and a maximum injection time of 3 ms.

RAW files were analyzed with Proteome Discoverer (version 3.1.0.638, Thermo Scientific) using Chimerys and fragment ion quantification with standard settings. Spectra were searched against the Swissprot human database containing only reviewed canonical and isoform sequences (release 2023_10; 42,359 entries). Carbamidomethylation (C) and oxidation (M) were selected as static and variable modifications, respectively, and identifications were filtered for 1%FDR at protein and peptide level. For quantitation, the “match-between-runs” option was selected, normalization was performed on total peptide amount using all peptides and protein abundances were calculated using summed abundances. The mass spectrometry proteomics data have been deposited to the ProteomeXchange Consortium via the PRIDE46 partner repository with the dataset identifier PXD067850. Data are available via ProteomeXchange with identifier PXD067850.

sec.title: Annexin V-FITC cell death assay
sec.p: Cells were seeded in 6 well plates. After treatment, cells were washed and collected in 500ul of Annexin V binding buffer (Abcam, ab14085). 5 μl of FITC bound Annexin V and PI obtained from the kit were added and incubated in dark for 5 min. Cells were then analysed on flow cytometer (AttuneNxT) and FlowJo v10.

sec.title: Oxidative stress experiments
sec.p: CellROX green Flow cytometry Assay kit (Thermofisher, C10492) was used to measure the level of ROS in cells. Cells were seeded in 6-well plates. After 2–3 days of treatment, cells were collected in 1 ml of culture media. 200 μM Tert-butyl hydroperoxide was used as positive control for inducing oxidative stress (provided in the kit). CellROX green reagent (750 nM) was added for 1 h at 37 oC. In the last 15 min, SYTOX Red dead cell stain (5 nM) was added to exclude dead cells from analysis. Cells were immediately measured using flow cytometer. Excitation and emission wavelengths for CellROX Green are 488 nm and 530/30 BP filter, respectively. Excitation and emission wavelengths for SYTOX Red are 639 nm and 660/20 BP filter respectively. Data was analysed using FlowJo v10.

sec.title: Statistics and reproducibility
sec.p: All data is shown as individual data points and expressed as mean ± SD. Statistical analysis was performed using GraphPad prism. Two-sided student’s t test was performed on biological replicates for cell line-based experiments. For mouse experiments, two-sided student’s t test was performed between the two groups compared. P value was denoted as follows: *p < 0.05, **p < 0.01, ***p < 0.001 and ****p < 0.0001. For all cell line-based experiments, n = 3 biological replicates were used. For animal studies, the number of samples was mentioned in figure legends. Each mouse sample was derived from a separate mouse. For mass-spectrometry experiment, n = 3 biological replicates for each condition were used. For RNA-sequencing experiment n = 2 biological replicates for each condition were used. Biological replicates are defined as samples derived from independent experiments.
